placeholders.name: PASTE YOUR EXISTING TEMPLATES/DRAFTS, OR DESCRIBE THE SITUATIONS: policy explanation, renewal reminder, follow-up, policy comparison, claims update, objection response, needs-analysis questions
placeholders.what: This is where you either paste the actual drafts you've already built (from earlier lessons or your own past messages) or, if you don't have drafts yet for a situation, just describe it in a sentence so the AI knows to draft one from scratch. Include as many of your real, already-used templates as you can, the more real content you give it, the less the AI has to invent.
examples: Policy explanation: [paste your homeowners exclusions explanation draft]. Renewal reminder: [paste your friendly-brief renewal template]. Claims update: don't have one yet, please draft using the claims-communication guardrails, empathetic acknowledgment first, facts stated exactly, no overpromising language.

I don't have written templates yet, just describe the situations I need: policy explanation for auto and homeowners clients, renewal reminders (routine and lapse-warning versions), post-quote check-ins, and objection responses for the 'found it cheaper elsewhere' objection.

Follow-up: [paste your missing-document follow-up draft]. Policy comparison: [paste your current-vs-renewal comparison table format]. Objection response: [paste your price-objection talking points from last month]. Needs-analysis questions: don't have a set yet, please draft open-ended questions for first-time homeowners.

variations.label: Building the library from scratch with no existing drafts
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you're starting the library for the first time and don't have any existing drafts to organize yet, you're generating the full set fresh, not just organizing what you already have.
variations.prompt:
Help me build a personal library of client-communication templates from scratch, I don't have existing drafts yet. Here are the situations I need to cover: [LIST YOUR SITUATIONS, e.g. policy explanation, renewal reminder, follow-up, policy comparison, claims update, objection response, needs-analysis questions]

For each one, draft a template using these guardrails: use only facts supplied via placeholders, never invent dates or figures, keep exclusions as prominent as coverage, no pressure or urgency tactics, empathetic acknowledgment before facts for anything claims-related. Include: 1) a short name and one-line description of when to use it, 2) the template with clearly marked placeholders, 3) a verification checkpoint before sending, 4) tone notes.

Then give me a short index of all templates by name and one-line description.

variations.label: Auditing and pruning an existing library that's gotten stale
variations.whenToUse: Use this periodically, for example quarterly, once you already have a library, to review which templates are still accurate and which need retiring or updating due to product, carrier, or regulation changes.
variations.prompt:
Here is my current template library:

[PASTE YOUR CURRENT LIBRARY]

Help me audit it. For each template, tell me: 1) whether the verification checkpoint is still specific and useful or has gotten vague, 2) whether anything in the tone notes or structure seems outdated, 3) flag any template that seems unused or redundant with another one for me to consider retiring. Do not rewrite the content itself yet, just flag what needs review, and I'll decide what to update.

variations.label: Building a smaller, role-specific subset for a new hire
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you're training a new agent and want to hand them a starter subset of the library, the highest-priority templates only, rather than the full set at once.
variations.prompt:
From my full template library below, help me build a smaller starter set of just the 4-5 highest-priority templates a brand new agent should learn first.

Full library:
[PASTE YOUR CURRENT LIBRARY]

For each of the 4-5 you select, keep the template, placeholders, verification checkpoint, and tone notes exactly as they are, do not rewrite the content, just select and organize the subset with a short note on why each one is a priority for someone new.

followUps.label: Make sure it didn't invent template types you don't need
followUps.prompt: List every template type in the output. Confirm each one matches a situation I actually described or provided a draft for, flag any you added that I didn't ask for, so I can decide whether to keep or remove them.

followUps.label: Check every verification checkpoint is specific, not generic
followUps.prompt: Go through each template's verification checkpoint and tell me if any of them are too vague to actually follow under time pressure, like just saying 'check for accuracy.' Rewrite the vague ones to name the specific thing to check and against what source.

followUps.label: Confirm the guardrails carried over from the original drafts
followUps.prompt: For each template that came from a draft I pasted, confirm the core guardrail from that situation is still present, for example, exclusions given equal weight to coverage in the policy explanation template, or no pressure language in the objection response template. Flag any that got softened or dropped in the reorganization.

followUps.label: Shorten the index so it's actually scannable
followUps.prompt: The index is too long to scan quickly under time pressure. Cut each entry's description down to under 10 words, grouped by category (renewals, claims, objections, etc.) so I can find the right one in a few seconds.

ins-a1-client-communication-template-lib.walkthrough:
Oscar is an insurance agent who has been through this entire lesson path over the past few weeks and now has several one-off drafts scattered across old emails and a notes app: a homeowners policy explanation, a renewal reminder template, and a claims-delay message he wrote during a busy week. He wants them organized somewhere he'll actually use them.

He opens Claude and pastes his three existing drafts under the lesson's placeholder, along with a note that he doesn't yet have anything for objection responses or needs-analysis questions and would like those drafted using the same guardrails.

Claude returns five organized entries. The homeowners policy explanation becomes "Homeowners Coverage Explainer" with placeholders like [POLICY SECTION], a verification checkpoint reading "re-check exclusion wording against current specimen policy before each use," and a tone note to keep exclusions as prominent as coverage. The two new ones, objection response and needs-analysis questions, get drafted fresh, following the non-pressuring, open-ended-questions guardrails from earlier lessons. A short index lists all five by name and one-line description.

Oscar runs the follow-up asking whether any verification checkpoint is too vague. Two of them just say "check for accuracy," so he asks Claude to make them specific, one becomes "confirm renewal date and premium against system of record," the other "confirm claim figures against claims system before sending."

He saves the finished library, with its index, as a Claude Project so he can bring new client-specific facts to any template without rebuilding the prompt each time. He sets a recurring quarterly reminder to review it. Building the initial library took about thirty-five minutes, replacing what used to be several disconnected documents he half-remembered where to find.
